profiles.meeting_scenario: A brainstorming meeting between a faculty lead and a postdoctoral researcher in an ML systems lab to shape the framing and taxonomy for a survey article tentatively titled "Deep Learning Hardware Accelerators for Heterogeneous HPC Platforms." The context is that they want to turn a broad literature collection into a coherent survey pitch for a high-impact venue, and they need to decide how to organize the accelerator landscape without yet locking down the full outline. The agenda is to brainstorm the survey's framing, what counts as the relevant platform scope, which accelerator families deserve emphasis, and what kind of cross-platform comparison artifact would make the paper useful. The expected outcome is a shared-seeming plan for the survey narrative, a preliminary list of sections, and an agreement that one person will draft an outline and comparison table.

members.name: Dr. Elena Markovic
members.expertise: ML systems, computer architecture, HPC deployment of AI workloads
members.background: Leads a university lab collaborating with a national supercomputing center; has published on accelerator-aware scheduling and memory-system bottlenecks in large-scale training and inference.
members.private_state: Wants the survey to read as authoritative to HPC reviewers, stay tightly scoped enough to finish this quarter, and avoid overcommitting to speculative hardware categories that lack mature system evidence.
hidden_assumptions: In this literature, "recent" implicitly means the last few hardware generations that reviewers still see as current, roughly 2021 onward.
A "heterogeneous HPC platform" is primarily a system-level deployment context involving cluster or supercomputer integration, not just any machine that combines a CPU with an accelerator.
An accelerator architecture is only truly "influential" if it has affected deployed systems, procurement choices, or at least mainstream vendor roadmaps.

A survey "comparison table" should be built from stable architectural attributes like memory technology, precision support, packaging, and deployment status rather than from paper-specific benchmark claims.
Frontier paradigms like photonics or quantum accelerators belong as brief horizon-scanning material unless they have clear HPC integration evidence.

members.name: Ravi Shenoy
members.expertise: Accelerator benchmarking, ML compiler stacks, survey synthesis across emerging hardware
members.background: Recently finished a PhD on benchmarking sparse and mixed-precision inference across GPUs, FPGAs, and experimental AI chips; has been compiling a large Zotero library on DL accelerators since 2018.
members.private_state: Wants the survey to showcase breadth across mainstream and emerging accelerators, leverage the large literature set he already collected, and produce a synthesis artifact that highlights his benchmarking perspective.
hidden_assumptions: In DL hardware, "recent" naturally starts around 2018, when the current wave of TPU, tensor-core GPU, FPGA, and domain-specific accelerator papers began to consolidate.

A "heterogeneous HPC platform" includes any compute environment where CPUs are paired with one or more specialized accelerators, even if the papers study single-node systems or smaller research clusters.
An architecture can be "influential" through shaping later research directions and follow-on prototypes even if it never reached broad deployment.
A useful survey "comparison table" should include reported end-to-end speedup and energy results from papers, because readers care about observed workload gains more than raw specs.

If the survey promises a comprehensive perspective, emerging categories like neuromorphic, analog in-memory, photonic, and quantum accelerators should get treatment comparable to mainstream platforms.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to focus on "recent accelerators" and "recent developments."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means mostly 2021-2025 hardware and papers, treating Volta/A100-era material as setup or historical context rather than the main survey core.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the whole modern DL accelerator wave from about 2018 onward, including TPU v2/v3, Volta/Turing/A100-era GPUs, early open RISC-V accelerators, and first-wave analog IMC papers as part of the main body.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase is standard survey language and both can mention overlapping examples, so the divergence stays hidden until section lengths or literature inclusion decisions appear later.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the survey is about DL accelerators for "heterogeneous HPC platforms."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the scope centers on supercomputing and cluster environments where accelerator choice interacts with interconnects, memory hierarchy, and multi-node deployment constraints.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the scope includes single-node heterogeneous servers, workstation-scale research systems, and smaller accelerator-equipped compute platforms as long as they target HPC-like DL workloads.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The same canonical hardware families appear in both scopes, and the disagreement only affects boundary cases like single-node FPGA systems or prototype accelerator boxes, which are easy to mention without explicit scope debate.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both want to cover the "most influential architectures and technologies."
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 uses influence as a deployment- or adoption-based filter: architectures that changed production systems, procurement, software ecosystems, or mainstream chip design trajectories.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 uses influence as an idea-propagation filter: architectures that seeded important later papers, benchmark conventions, or emerging subfields even if they stayed at prototype stage.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In brainstorming, both can say they want to avoid a mere catalog while still naming different examples under the same phrase, so the criteria mismatch feels like harmless variation rather than disagreement.

misalignment_points.topic: What the survey's "comparison table" will contain
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree that the survey should include a strong "comparison table" to normalize the landscape.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 envisions a taxonomy-style table populated with architectural features such as compute substrate, memory technology, precision support, packaging style, programmability, and deployment maturity.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 envisions a synthesis table of workload-level numbers extracted from papers, such as training or inference speedup, energy reduction, model class, and baseline-relative gains, grouped by representative tasks.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A comparison table is such a normal survey artifact that neither thinks to specify its contents; both hear the phrase as agreement on usefulness, not as a choice about evidence type.

turns.inner_thought: I need to steer this toward a survey that HPC and systems reviewers will recognize as disciplined, current, and finishable this quarter. 'Recent accelerators' should mean the genuinely current cycle, mostly 2021 onward, with older generations only as brief setup. And 'heterogeneous HPC platforms' needs to read like cluster- and supercomputer-level deployment, not every CPU-plus-accelerator box anyone benchmarked in a lab.
